title: The JSON that was almost JSON

terminal.description: A shell in your workspace, already pointed at the offline lab model.

tasks.title: Crash the parser on purpose
tasks.description:
In `src/reproduce.ts`, implement `reproduceCrash()`.

Pick a customer message from `src/messages.ts` that makes the original `parseRequest` throw. Call `parseRequest` with it, catch the error, and return:

- `message`: the customer message you sent
- `error`: the message of the error that was thrown

The check runs your function against the original `parse.ts` and then confirms your message really crashes it.
nextSteps: Run `node src/demo.ts` and see which messages end in an error.
Call `parseRequest` with one of them inside a `try` block.
Return the customer message and the caught error's message.
hints: The demo prints a line for every message in messages.ts. Some of them do not come back as results.
A caught value is typed `unknown`. Treat it as an `Error` to read its `message`.
The fenced and chatty messages both make JSON.parse throw. Either one works; return its text and `err.message`.

tasks.title: Stop trusting the model's JSON
tasks.description:
Fix `parseRequest` in `src/parse.ts` so a strange reply can never crash the endpoint or slip a bad request through.

It must:

- find the JSON object even when the model wraps it in a code fence or puts a sentence before it
- never throw because of the reply text; resolve to `{ ok: false, reason }` instead
- only return `{ ok: true, request }` when `action` is one of `reschedule`, `redirect`, `cancel` and `trackingId` looks like `KP-` followed by 5 digits

Keep the exported types and the function signature.
nextSteps: Print the raw reply text for each message and look at what surrounds the JSON.
Pull out the part of the text that is the JSON object.
Parse it so a failure becomes `{ ok: false }`, not an exception.
Check `action` and `trackingId` before returning `ok: true`, then run the demo.
hints: There are two separate problems: getting the JSON out of the text, and deciding whether what you got is a request you can act on.
The JSON object starts at the first `{` and ends at the last `}`. JSON.parse can still fail, so give it a try/catch.
`as DeliveryRequest` only silences the compiler. Write a small function that checks the type of each field and returns a boolean.

tasks.title: Write the test that would have caught it
tasks.description:
Write vitest tests in `src/parse.test.ts` that check:

- a reply wrapped in a code fence, or with chatty text around the JSON, still parses
- a message with no delivery request resolves to `{ ok: false }` instead of throwing
- a reply with the wrong shape (no tracking id, or an action Kes does not support) resolves to `{ ok: false }`

The check runs your test file beside the original `parse.ts` (it must fail), beside a correct fix (it must pass) and beside a fix that parses safely but never checks the shape (it must fail).
nextSteps: Write one test per kind of reply: fenced, chatty, no JSON, wrong shape.
Run `npx vitest run src/parse.test.ts` against your fixed code.
Ask which of your tests a fix without shape checks would still pass.
hints: Each entry in messages.ts makes the lab model answer in a different way. Use them as your cases.
Assert on `result.ok` first; that is the part of the contract callers rely on.
A version that only adds try/catch passes the fenced and no-JSON cases. The missingId and unknownAction messages are what catch it.
